nameStory: The name 'cornelian cherry' comes from the Latin 'cornum,' meaning horn, referring to the incredibly hard, dense wood that was prized for making spear tips and tool handles in ancient times. The 'cherry' part refers to the bright red, cherry-like fruits, though this plant isn't actually related to true cherries at all!
description: Cornelian cherry is a small deciduous tree or large shrub that grows 15-25 feet tall, originally from Europe but occasionally planted in New England gardens. It's a member of the dogwood family but looks quite different from our familiar flowering dogwood. This early bloomer produces clusters of tiny yellow flowers before its leaves emerge, followed by bright red oval fruits in late summer.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright yellow flowers appear in dense rounded clusters in very early spring, often in March before leaves emerge. Each cluster contains 15-25 individual flowers that feel papery when touched and have a faint sweet scent.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves are 3-4 inches long with prominent parallel veins curving toward the tip, typical of dogwoods. They feel smooth on top but slightly fuzzy underneath, and turn yellow to reddish in fall.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red oval fruits about 3/4 inch long ripen in late summer, hanging like tiny cherries. They're edible but quite tart and contain a large hard pit that rattles when shaken.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Mature bark is grayish-brown and develops a distinctive flaky, scaly texture that you can pick at with your fingernails. Younger branches are smooth and reddish-brown.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a small rounded tree or large multi-stemmed shrub with an open, somewhat irregular crown. Branches tend to be somewhat zigzagged rather than perfectly straight.

habitat: In New England, cornelian cherry is found almost exclusively in cultivated settings like botanical gardens, arboretums, and the yards of plant enthusiasts. It prefers well-drained soils and full sun to partial shade, and is quite hardy once established.

seasonality.spring: The star season for identification - bright yellow flower clusters bloom in March or early April before leaves appear, making it unmistakable among our native plants.
seasonality.summer: Green oval leaves with dogwood-family venation provide identification clues, and small green fruits begin developing by midsummer.
seasonality.fall: Bright red cherry-like fruits ripen and leaves turn yellow to reddish before dropping, revealing the distinctive flaky bark pattern.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the characteristic dogwood opposite branching pattern, and the scaly bark becomes more prominent for identification.

funFact: The wood of cornelian cherry is so incredibly dense that it actually sinks in water - it was the preferred material for making butcher's mallets because it wouldn't split or dent even under heavy use!
confusionNotes: The early yellow flowers might remind you of witch hazel, but witch hazel blooms in fall and has ribbon-like petals, while cornelian cherry has tiny rounded flowers in dense clusters. The red fruits could be confused with cherries, but these are much more tart and have the distinctive dogwood leaf venation.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name, cornelian cherry isn't related to true cherries at all - it's a dogwood that just happens to have cherry-like red fruits. This naming confusion is common with many plants that were named for their superficial resemblance to more familiar species.
compareHints: Unlike our native flowering dogwood with its large white bracts, cornelian cherry has tiny yellow flowers in clusters. It's also much earlier blooming than other dogwoods and is the only common dogwood in New England that produces edible red fruits. The flowers appear before leaves emerge, which is unusual among our dogwood family members.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its tree and shrub dogwood relatives, Canadian bunchberry is the only dogwood in New England that grows as a tiny herbaceous perennial on the forest floor.
Among dogwoods, this is the only one in New England with alternate leaves - all others have opposite leaves.
Among New England's dogwoods, red osier is the wetland specialist with the most colorful bark.
Among New England's dogwoods, silky dogwood is unique for its distinctly fuzzy leaf undersides - run your finger underneath any dogwood leaf, and only silky dogwood will feel soft and velvety.
Among New England's dogwoods, flowering dogwood is unique for its large, showy white bracts and tree-like size.

Among New England's dogwoods, gray dogwood is unique for its white berries on red stems - flowering dogwood has red berries, red osier dogwood has white berries on white stems, and silky dogwood has blue berries.
Among New England dogwoods, round-leaved dogwood is unique for its combination of rounded leaf tips and rough leaf texture.
Among dogwoods, kousa is unique for its late bloom time, pointed bracts, and strawberry-like fruits.

Among New England dogwoods, blue-fruited dogwood is distinguished by its true blue berries - red osier dogwood has white berries, gray dogwood has white berries on red stems, and silky dogwood has blue-white berries.
Among New England dogwoods, roughleaf dogwood is unique for its sandpaper-textured leaves - no other dogwood species in our region has this distinctive rough feel.
Common dogwood stands out from other New England dogwoods primarily by its intensely colored winter stems - most of our native dogwoods have gray, brown, or only mildly reddish winter bark.

Among dogwoods, Tatarian dogwood's red stems are most similar to native red osier dogwood, but Tatarian tends to have more orange-red coloring and is found in drier garden settings rather than wetlands.

Korean cornel dogwood differs from most other dogwoods in New England by blooming very early with small yellow flowers rather than white ones, and by producing oval red fruits rather than round blue or white berries.
